questions.question: What is a Savings Plan and how does it differ from Reserved Instances?
questions.answer: A Savings Plan is a flexible pricing commitment where you pledge to spend a specific dollar amount per hour for 1 or 3 years, receiving up to 72% discount. Unlike Reserved Instances, which lock you to a specific instance type, region, and OS, Savings Plans apply automatically to any matching usage. Compute Savings Plans are even broader — they cover EC2, Lambda, and Fargate.

questions.question: What are the three types of Savings Plans and how do they differ?
questions.answer: 1. Compute Savings Plans: Most flexible — applies to any EC2 instance (any family, size, OS, region) plus Fargate and Lambda. Up to 66% discount. 2. EC2 Instance Savings Plans: Locked to a specific instance family and region (e.g., t3 in us-east-1) but flexible within that family. Up to 72% discount. 3. SageMaker Savings Plans: Only for Amazon SageMaker ML workloads.

questions.question: What happens to a Spot Instance when AWS needs the capacity back?
questions.answer: AWS sends a 2-minute interruption notice to the instance (via instance metadata and EventBridge). After 2 minutes, the instance is interrupted according to the configured behavior: Terminate (deleted), Stop (stopped, storage preserved), or Hibernate (RAM saved to EBS, then stopped). Applications should be designed to handle this gracefully.

questions.question: What are the three Spot Instance interruption behaviors and when would you use each?
questions.answer: 1. Terminate (default): Instance is deleted. Use for stateless jobs where you can simply restart from scratch. 2. Stop: Instance is stopped, EBS root volume preserved. Use when you want to resume the exact instance state without losing storage. Requires a persistent Spot request. 3. Hibernate: RAM written to encrypted EBS root, then instance stops. On restart, RAM is reloaded and applications resume exactly where they left off. Use for in-memory applications or long-running jobs.

questions.question: What is a Dedicated Host and why would a company use one?
questions.answer: A Dedicated Host is a physical EC2 server fully allocated to your use — no other AWS customer shares the hardware. Companies use it for: 1) BYOL (Bring Your Own License) for software licensed per physical core or socket (like Oracle or Windows Server). 2) Compliance requirements mandating physical isolation. 3) Visibility and control over hardware placement for licensing management.

questions.question: What is the maximum discount available for each EC2 pricing model?
questions.answer: On-Demand: 0% (baseline price). Reserved Instances: up to 72% (3-year, All Upfront). Savings Plans: up to 72% (EC2 Instance SP) or 66% (Compute SP). Spot Instances: up to 90% (highest possible discount). Dedicated Hosts: variable — On-Demand host pricing plus optional Reserved discount.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a Dedicated Host and a Dedicated Instance?
questions.answer: Dedicated Hosts: You get an entire physical server. You can see the physical core and socket topology. Supports full BYOL licensing. You control instance placement on the host. Billed per host per hour. Dedicated Instances: Your instances run on hardware isolated to your account, but you don't see physical topology. Limited BYOL support. No placement control. Billed per instance. Use Dedicated Host when you need BYOL or physical core visibility. Use Dedicated Instance for basic account-level isolation.

questions.question: What is a Spot Fleet?
questions.answer: A Spot Fleet is a managed group of Spot Instances (and optionally On-Demand Instances) that work together to meet a target capacity. You specify multiple instance types and AZs — AWS automatically picks the cheapest available combination. If one pool becomes unavailable or expensive, the fleet shifts to another. This diversification strategy reduces interruption risk compared to using a single instance type in a single AZ.

questions.question: What are the three payment options for Savings Plans and how do they compare?
questions.answer: All Upfront: Pay full commitment amount at purchase. Highest discount. Best if you have the capital and want maximum savings. Partial Upfront: Pay some upfront, rest monthly. Mid-level discount. Balances capital outlay with savings. No Upfront: Pay nothing at purchase, charged monthly. Lowest discount among commitment options. Best when cash flow is a concern. All options are available for both 1-year and 3-year terms.

questions.question: When should you use On-Demand vs Savings Plans vs Spot Instances?
questions.answer: On-Demand: Unpredictable usage, short-term projects, dev/test environments, applications you can't interrupt. No commitment needed. Savings Plans: Steady, predictable workloads you'll run for 1+ years. You get a discount without locking to a specific instance type. Spot Instances: Fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads like batch processing, ML training, CI/CD. You want maximum savings (up to 90%) and can handle interruptions.

questions.question: Describe a real-world scenario where you recommended Spot Instances and how you handled the interruption risk.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our team ran nightly ETL jobs processing 500GB of log data. On-Demand costs were $800/month. (Task) Reduce costs without compromising job completion. (Action) Migrated to a Spot Fleet across three instance types and two AZs. Enabled checkpointing every 15 minutes using S3 to save progress. Set interruption behavior to Terminate with restart logic — if a job failed, it requeued and resumed from the last checkpoint. (Result) Monthly costs dropped to under $100 — 87% savings. Interruptions occurred twice in 3 months, adding less than 30 minutes total delay.

questions.question: Walk me through how you would determine the right commitment amount for a Savings Plan.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our company wanted to optimize $50K/month in EC2 On-Demand spend. (Task) Choose the right Savings Plan commitment to maximize savings without over-committing. (Action) 1. Opened AWS Cost Explorer, navigated to Savings Plans Recommendations. 2. Set lookback period to 30 days and commitment term to 1 year. 3. Reviewed the recommended hourly commitment and projected savings. 4. Cross-verified using the AWS Pricing Calculator by inputting our instance types and comparing On-Demand vs Savings Plan costs. 5. Committed to 75% of baseline usage (leaving 25% on On-Demand for flexibility). (Result) Achieved 42% average cost reduction — saving $21K/month while retaining flexibility for usage spikes.

questions.question: A client has an Oracle Database on-premises with per-core licenses. They want to migrate to AWS. How would you advise them on EC2 tenancy?
questions.answer: (Situation) Client has Oracle Standard Edition 2 with per-physical-core licensing — cannot move to shared instances because Oracle requires knowing the physical core count. (Task) Find the right AWS EC2 option for BYOL compliance. (Action) Recommended Dedicated Hosts with Dedicated tenancy. This gives the client full visibility into the physical core and socket count on the host. We verified the host's physical core configuration in the EC2 console. Configured the host with the minimum number of cores needed for their workload to minimize license consumption. (Result) Client successfully migrated Oracle to AWS using existing licenses — no new Oracle license purchase needed. Saved approximately $200K in licensing costs.

questions.question: How would you design a cost-optimized EC2 strategy for a company with mixed workload types?
questions.answer: (Situation) A company had 4 workload types: steady web servers (24/7), nightly batch jobs (4 hours/night), compliance-sensitive database, and irregular dev/test servers. (Task) Design a pricing strategy minimizing cost while meeting each workload's needs. (Action) Web servers → EC2 Instance Savings Plan (1-year, Partial Upfront): predictable usage, ~65% savings. Batch jobs → Spot Fleet with checkpointing: interruptible, ~85% savings. Compliance database → Dedicated Instances for account-level isolation. Dev/test → On-Demand: unpredictable, no commitment needed. (Result) Overall EC2 bill reduced by approximately 55% while maintaining reliability and compliance for each tier.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you used the AWS Pricing Calculator for a cloud cost decision.
questions.answer: (Situation) Team debated whether to use Reserved Instances or Savings Plans for new EC2 deployment. (Task) Provide data-driven recommendation. (Action) Opened calculator.aws, created three estimates: 1) On-Demand baseline for 20 t3.large instances, 2) EC2 Instance Savings Plan 1-year no upfront, 3) Compute Savings Plan 1-year no upfront. Compared monthly and annual costs side by side. Also factored in that the team planned to add Lambda functions in Q3 — Compute SP would cover those too. (Result) Recommended Compute Savings Plan — $800/month more expensive than EC2 Instance SP, but the Lambda coverage would save an additional $1,200/month when Lambda workloads launched. Net benefit: $400/month advantage with more flexibility.

questions.question: A Spot Fleet was running fine for weeks, then suddenly all instances were terminated simultaneously. What likely happened and how would you prevent it?
questions.answer: (Situation) A Spot Fleet using t3.large instances in a single AZ was interrupted entirely at once. (Task) Diagnose and prevent recurrence. (Action) Root cause: The fleet was not diversified — single instance type in single AZ. When demand surged in that AZ, all capacity was reclaimed simultaneously. Fix: 1. Configured the fleet to use t3.large, t3.xlarge, and m5.large (multiple families). 2. Spread across us-east-1a, 1b, and 1c. 3. Added 20% On-Demand buffer via 'maintain' fleet request type for minimum guaranteed capacity. 4. Used Spot Instance Advisor to verify low interruption frequency for chosen instance types. (Result) No complete outage since. Maximum observed interruption: 2 out of 15 instances at once, easily absorbed by remaining capacity.

questions.question: Explain the Spot Instance hibernation feature. When would you use it over Stop?
questions.answer: Both Stop and Hibernate preserve the EBS root volume when a Spot Instance is interrupted. The difference: Stop simply halts the instance — RAM contents are lost. When restarted, the OS boots fresh and applications restart from zero (loading data from disk). Hibernate writes the entire RAM contents to the encrypted EBS root volume before stopping. When restarted, RAM is reloaded — the OS and all applications resume exactly where they paused, mid-execution. Use Hibernate when: your application has expensive in-memory state that takes a long time to rebuild (e.g., cached datasets loaded into RAM), and the restart overhead would be significant. Requirement: the root EBS volume must be encrypted. Use Stop when: you just need storage to survive (no RAM state needed), or your instance type/size doesn't support Hibernate.

questions.question: How do you monitor and act on Spot interruption notices in a production batch system?
questions.answer: (Situation) Running a Spot-based batch cluster processing financial data. Needed graceful handling of interruptions. (Task) Build a system that handles Spot interruptions without data loss. (Action) 1. Used EC2 Instance Metadata Service endpoint to poll for interruption notices every 5 seconds. 2. Set up Amazon EventBridge rule to capture EC2 Spot Instance interruption warning events. 3. EventBridge triggered a Lambda function that: checkpointed current job progress to S3, sent the remaining work back to an SQS queue, logged the interruption event to CloudWatch. 4. New Spot Instances (or fallback On-Demand) picked up from SQS and resumed from checkpoint. (Result) Zero data loss across 6 months of operation despite 23 interruptions. Maximum job delay per interruption: under 5 minutes.

questions.question: What happens if your usage exceeds the amount covered by your Savings Plan?
questions.answer: Savings Plans apply a discount up to your committed hourly amount. Any usage beyond the committed amount is automatically charged at On-Demand rates. For example, if you committed $0.10/hour and your actual usage in an hour totals $0.15/hour, $0.10 receives the discounted rate and $0.05 is charged at On-Demand pricing. This means under-commitment costs you the On-Demand rate for the excess, while over-commitment (committing more than you use) means you pay for unused commitment.

questions.question: A company's Savings Plan recommendation shows 80% coverage of their EC2 usage. Should they commit to 100% coverage? Why or why not?
questions.answer: (Situation) Recommendations suggested committing to cover 80% of current usage. Management asked whether to go to 100%. (Task) Advise on commitment level. (Action) Advised against 100% commitment for these reasons: 1. Usage fluctuates — even 'stable' workloads have variation. Committing 100% means paying for committed capacity even if usage drops. 2. Business changes — instances may be terminated, rightsized, or migrated to Lambda/containers. Committed spend continues regardless. 3. Standard best practice: commit 70–80% of baseline, keep 20–30% On-Demand for flexibility. (Result) Company committed 78% — saved 58% overall on covered instances while maintaining flexibility to scale down without stranded commitment costs.

questions.question: Compare Compute Savings Plans vs EC2 Instance Savings Plans from an architectural decision perspective. When would you choose each?
questions.answer: Choose EC2 Instance Savings Plans when: your instance family won't change for the commitment period, you want the maximum 72% discount, and your workload is strictly EC2. Common for mature, stable production environments with known instance requirements. Choose Compute Savings Plans when: you're modernizing (might shift to Lambda or Fargate), you need instance family flexibility (might change from t3 to t4g or m5), or you have a diverse mix of EC2 + serverless. The 6% lower maximum discount (66% vs 72%) is usually worth it for the architectural flexibility. In practice, many companies use Compute SPs as their primary coverage because the flexibility enables future cloud-native migrations without stranded commitments.

questions.question: Design a cost optimization architecture for a SaaS company with unpredictable traffic spikes, steady background processing, and strict compliance requirements for payment data.
questions.answer: The architecture would use three EC2 tiers with different pricing: 1) Payment processing servers (compliance requirement) → Dedicated Instances for account-level physical isolation. Use EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the steady component, On-Demand for burst. 2) Application servers (variable traffic) → Auto Scaling group with a mix: Savings Plan baseline for minimum capacity + On-Demand for predictable growth + Spot Instances (with ALB health checks) for burst capacity. Set Spot weight lower in the ASG launch template. 3) Background batch processing → Pure Spot Fleet with diversification across 5+ instance types and 3 AZs. Implement SQS-based job queue with checkpointing. Overall result: payment tier ~55% savings, app tier ~40% average savings, batch tier ~85% savings. Compliance maintained, availability protected via multi-tier strategy.

questions.question: How would you architect a machine learning training infrastructure using Spot Instances to maximize cost savings while minimizing training time loss from interruptions?
questions.answer: Key design principles: 1) Spot Fleet diversification: Use 6+ instance types across GPU families (p3.2xlarge, p3.8xlarge, g4dn.xlarge, g4dn.2xlarge) across 3+ AZs. GPU Spot pools have lower interruption rates when diversified. 2) Checkpointing strategy: Configure training framework (PyTorch/TensorFlow) to checkpoint to S3 every N steps — typically every 5–10 minutes for long jobs. 3) Auto-resume: Use EC2 Auto Recovery + SQS job queue. On interruption (EventBridge event), push remaining job to SQS. New instance pulls from queue and resumes from latest S3 checkpoint. 4) Instance selection: Use Spot Instance Advisor to pre-filter to pools with <10% interruption frequency. Prioritize p3 family for consistent pricing history. 5) Fallback: Configure Spot Fleet with On-Demand fallback for final epoch if training is near completion to avoid restarting long jobs. Result: 70–85% cost reduction vs On-Demand GPU instances, typically <5 minutes lost per interruption.

questions.question: A company purchased a 1-year Compute Savings Plan 6 months ago but has since reduced their EC2 fleet by 40%. What are their options and what would you advise?
questions.answer: Important fact: Savings Plans cannot be cancelled. The commitment runs for the full term regardless of usage. Options available: 1) List the Savings Plan on the AWS Marketplace for sale to another customer — the most direct option to recover unused value. Note: only supported for certain plan types. 2) Apply the remaining commitment to other eligible services — since it's a Compute SP, any EC2, Lambda, or Fargate usage in the account can absorb the committed spend. Review whether other teams or workloads can use this capacity. 3) If within an AWS Organization, verify whether the Savings Plan applies across other accounts in the Org — SPs can be shared organization-wide. 4) Future prevention: Never commit 100% of usage. Always leave 20–30% on On-Demand as a buffer against workload reductions. Use Cost Explorer to review coverage vs commitment monthly.

questions.question: Explain how AWS determines which Savings Plan to apply first when a customer has multiple overlapping plans.
questions.answer: When a customer has multiple Savings Plans, AWS applies them in a specific order to maximize the customer's benefit: 1) EC2 Instance Savings Plans are applied first because they offer the deepest discount for matching usage. AWS wants to ensure the highest-discount plans are used to their full potential before falling back to more flexible plans. 2) Compute Savings Plans are applied next to cover any remaining eligible usage that the EC2 Instance SP didn't cover (including Lambda and Fargate). 3) Any remaining usage after all Savings Plans are exhausted is charged at On-Demand rates. Within each type, plans with the highest discount are applied first. This automatic application happens on an hourly basis — you don't need to configure which plan covers which resource.
